userStories.title: Follow any playback end to end, and see why the cluster needed more workers
userStories.description: An operator must be able to see exactly where a playback stalled and why the cluster needed more workers, not only that a film is transcoding. Metrics (JS-019) give totals: stalls happened, the queue is deep. This adds one OpenTelemetry trace per playback (PlaySessionId) across the api, stream and worker processes: PlaybackInfo and its decision with reasons; each segment request and where its time went (served from the store, waited on a job, started a job); the job queued, claimed (queue time, which worker) and its ffmpeg runs with their speed; helpers started, and helpers wanted but not started for lack of a free slot; and a failover (lock lost, reap, replacement). The reasons for more workers become metrics too, which autoscaling (JS-057) scales on, so the reason it scaled is visible. Viewers keep seeing in their app that a film is transcoding and why (JS-067).
acceptanceCriteria: One trace per playback session spans the api, stream and worker processes, its context carried in the transcode job row across the Postgres handoff

Given a stalled segment (over 5 s), its trace shows which part took the time: waiting for a free slot, an encode slower than real time, the upload, or reading the store; the stall metric links to the trace (exemplar)
A failover shows the dead worker's span end and the replacement's begin in one trace
Helper decisions are traced and counted: helpers started with the job's speed, and helpers wanted but not started because no slot was free

Demand for workers is a metric with its reason (jobs waiting for a slot and how long, helpers wanted but refused, jobs below real time), and the autoscaler's input is one of these, so why the cluster grew can be read back
Log lines carry the trace id (JS-022), so a trace leads to its logs
jellyfin-web's playback info still shows transcoding, its reasons and speed (JS-067), and stays right while helpers run (the viewer's own job may have ended)
Exported over OTLP to any backend, off by default; the dogfood runs a backend and the docs show reading a stall from it
Checked with real processes: a test collector receives a playback's trace from three processes, with a stall and a failover in it
userStories.notes: Needs a design review; the homelab has no tracing backend yet (Tempo suggested). Product owner (2026-11-08): wants to trace everything through the pipeline, see where something stalled and why more workers were needed; placed before P6 (Kubernetes). JS-024 review (UX): Sessions can show the viewer's job as done while helpers encode, and no log line says a helper started.

The decision table tests cover every VideoRangeType against jellyfin-web's own profile conditions

userStories.title: Parallel transcoding of one stream across workers
userStories.description: When a job runs below about 1.2x real time, helper jobs on other workers encode later chunks of the same film, so CPU on every node serves one viewer. Deterministic segments let the chunks splice.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building (chunk boundaries, slots, cancellation, read-ahead, failover of a helper)
Three worker processes encode one film in chunks; the assembled segments equal a single worker's video byte for byte
hls.js plays through and seeks across chunk boundaries with no stall or discontinuity
A helper killed mid-chunk is replaced and the viewer keeps playing
Helpers never take the last free slot from a new viewer
Measured speedup with 1, 2 and 3 workers in the PR
userStories.notes: The user's idea: use CPU on all nodes rather than relying on a GPU. 'Gotta test sharding streams.' Built 2026-11-08: a job below 1.2x real time (judged after 2 s of output) inserts a helper row for the next free 4-segment chunk within the viewer's lead; helpers are claimed by other workers first and never take a worker's last free slot. A job's ffmpeg runs on across chunk starts until it reaches a chunk another job holds, so a job nobody helps is one ffmpeg. Measured with each worker's ffmpeg pinned to one CPU: 1 worker 16.3 s, 2 workers 10.4 s (1.57x), 3 workers 8.0 s (2.03x). Re-encoded segments from different runs have the same frames and frame times within 1 ms, not the same bytes (x264 stays multi-threaded). A burnt image subtitle gets no helpers (a run that starts mid-film loses the cue showing at its start); JS-071 closes that gap. A failed helper does not fail the viewer's spec and blocks re-helping its chunk for 30 s. Backlog: helpers are a fixed threshold (1.2x), not a measure of spare capacity across the cluster; a helper's chunk that the viewer never reaches is wasted work until the idle kill; per-helper metrics (JS-021 traces should show which chunks were helped and why).

userStories.title: Keep playback and transcodes through a Postgres failover
userStories.description: A CNPG switchover ends every worker's lock connection; today every transcode restarts. Re-lock first, then check the worker's own row: if it is present nobody touched its jobs and they continue. The stream role has the same failure: every playlist, segment and direct-play request reads Postgres (token, source row, viewer), and a database error is answered with a 500 (internal/api/server.go requireAuth, transcode.go, stream.go), which jellyfin-web treats as the end of playback (DOMAINS.md: any answer of 400 or more destroys the player). So a switchover, the most ordinary Kubernetes event, stops every viewer. The stream role must never answer 5xx for a database that is briefly away.
acceptanceCriteria: Postgres goes away and comes back before the jobs' leases run out (10 seconds from the last renewal, renewed every 3): every transcode job on every worker goes on, with three workers each running jobs and viewers asking for segments meanwhile; each job's row, worker and ffmpeg process are the same before and after, and no second job is started for its spec

That holds for a re-encode, a copy and a job paused at its lead, and for both shapes of 'away': every connection ended with new ones accepted at once (a switchover seen through a Service), and every connection ended with new ones refused for some seconds (a restart); in both the rows come back as they were and no advisory lock is held

Every worker's jobs survive, not only those of the first worker to lock again: nothing that looks for dead workers as Postgres returns (each worker's quarter-second reap, a PlaybackInfo on an api replica) forgets a live worker that is still taking its lock again

A segment finished while Postgres is away neither ends the job nor is lost: nothing is stored until the check before every store passes again (invariant 37), then the waiting segments are stored and the job goes on
No job ends `failed` because Postgres was away, and no spec is refused for it afterwards (no 'the last attempt failed' at PlaybackInfo or on a segment): a job the outage does cut short is `cancelled`

An outage that outlasts a job's lease: the worker stops that ffmpeg no later than it does today (its first heartbeat after the lease ran out), stores nothing from it afterwards, and the viewer's next segment request starts the job again at the first missing segment and is answered with the segment, not an error

A worker killed while Postgres is away is forgotten once Postgres is back, and another worker continues its job at the first missing segment; the viewer's request waiting on it is answered with the segment

A worker locks again first and only then looks for its own row: finding it gone (another replica took it for dead), it stops every ffmpeg and puts its row back only afterwards; while it does not hold the lock it claims no new job, however long locking again takes

A worker that cannot take its lock again while Postgres still answers its other queries, and that another replica has forgotten, stops its ffmpeg within the 1 second grace, before a replacement's ffmpeg starts, as a worker that lost its lock does today

No job is ever owned by two workers (invariant 25), shown with real processes under contention: over repeated rounds of ending one worker's lock connection, and of ending every worker's at once, while the other workers and a stream replica reap, the old owner's ffmpeg and a replacement's never run at once for one spec (helpers apart), no worker stores a segment after it was forgotten, and each round ends with the job still on its worker or with that worker's ffmpeg gone before the replacement's starts

While Postgres is away, for at least the 90 seconds a segment request may already wait (WaitTimeout), no stream-role request is answered 400 or more because of it; checked for each of the master playlist, the main playlist, the init segment, a stored segment, a segment its job has yet to make, a segment whose job was queued just before the outage (no 503 for a queue wait that passed while Postgres was away), and a direct-play range request, on two stream replicas with several viewers at once: each gets its usual answer and body, at once or when Postgres is back, and so does a request the player abandoned after 10 seconds and asked again

Postgres being away never lets a request in: one whose token belongs to no signed-in device gets no playlist, segment or film byte while it is away, also from a replica that was serving other viewers a moment before, and is answered 401 at the latest when Postgres is back

With Postgres up, whatever a stream replica keeps in memory is short-lived: a signed-out token is refused, and a film whose source row the scan has changed (a replaced file) is served from the new row, by every stream replica no later than 10 seconds after the change, and at once if the build keeps nothing

In jellyfin-web in the e2e tier, Postgres is restarted in the middle of a film playing as an HLS transcode, and the browser asks for at least one segment while it is away (the scenario counts them): the picture goes on past the point it had reached, with no dialog, the same player and no new PlaybackInfo, and no request the browser made, to either role, is answered 400 or more because of the database

The same in the e2e tier for a film that direct plays, with a seek while Postgres is away to a place the browser has not buffered, so that it must ask for a range: the picture plays on from there (once Postgres is back, at the latest), with no dialog, and no request the browser made is answered 400 or more because of the database

userStories.title: Use every GPU and CPU the cluster has
userStories.description: A worker uses whatever encoder hardware its node exposes (NVIDIA NVENC, Intel QSV or VAAPI, AMD VAAPI) and falls back to the CPU, so a cluster with GPUs uses them, as Jellyfin does on the dogfood's Intel iGPUs. fMP4 can't splice across encoder families (spikes/seam: x264 spliced with NVENC lost half the frames), so each stream is given the best family with room when it starts, and its helpers (JS-024) and failover stay in that family. A GPU can also serve a CPU-encoded stream by decoding for it, if its frames equal software decoding, so every node still helps every stream.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building: how a family is chosen for a stream, helpers and failover within a family, and what a viewer sees when the last worker of their stream's family is lost mid-film (playing on is the goal; a restart needs the product owner's decision); and whether a copy and a re-encode should share one slot pool (today a near-free copy holds a slot for the whole film like a multi-core re-encode)
A worker detects at start which encoders its node can run (a short test encode per family, not the ffmpeg build's list) and advertises them; a node with no GPU runs exactly as before
A new stream gets a GPU family when a worker of that family has a free slot, and the CPU otherwise; the encoder family stays in the spec hash and the decision is logged and metered with its reason
Helpers and failover of a GPU stream stay in its family; a seek, a restart and a helper's chunk splice cleanly on QSV/VAAPI and NVENC as the seam spike showed for one family
Hardware decoding for CPU-encoded streams only where its frames are measured equal to software decoding (per codec and family); otherwise software decoding

Tested on real hardware in its own tier chosen explicitly (never skipped): Intel QSV/VAAPI on the dogfood cluster's iGPUs and NVENC on a developer machine; jellyfin-web plays, seeks and recovers from a killed GPU worker
Operators see which encoder family and worker serve each stream (Sessions, metrics, JS-021 traces)
userStories.source: PRODUCT.md phase5-library; rewritten 2026-11-08: the product owner wants every GPU and CPU in the cluster used where possible, priority kept in P5
userStories.notes: The dogfood cluster has an Intel iGPU on each of its three nodes (gpu.intel.com/i915: 1 allocatable) and the user's Jellyfin requests one; the developer machine has an RTX 4070 Ti and an AMD iGPU. GPU tone mapping (libplacebo or vendor filters) gives frames unlike zscale's, so it splices only within its own family.

userStories.title: Burnt image subtitles in every run: helpers, seeks and failovers draw the cue that is showing
userStories.description: A PGS, VobSub or DVB cue is one packet when it appears, so an ffmpeg that begins mid-film (a seek, a failover, a helper's chunk) never sees the cue already on screen and leaves it out until the next one (DOMAINS 51's known departure). JS-024 therefore gives burnt image subtitles no helpers: a slow 4K film with Blu-ray subtitles stalls on one worker as before. PRODUCT.md (The experience we're building) promises that every film gets every capability. Make a run that begins at segment N draw the cue showing at N: start its ffmpeg early enough to read that cue's packet (the packet time comes from the track itself, read once and cached like the PGS file copy) and drop the frames before N, or another way that keeps the segment's frames at a single run's times. Then let burnt image subtitles be chunked and helped like any slow re-encode.
acceptanceCriteria: Every run that begins at a segment N > 0 inside a burnt image cue draws, from its first frame until the cue ends, the picture a run from zero draws there, for each of PGS, VobSub and DVB; shown for a seek, a failover restart and a helper's chunk, each through a worker's job (TestBurnedImageSubtitleIsAtTheRightTime without its known-departure case)

The same holds for a cue that began long before the cut (50 s or more, several chunks back), on a film the scan has read, with the cue times reaching the run as they do in production and never handed in by the test
The same holds for a film whose index the scan does not read today: MPEG-2 video with a VobSub track in Matroska (a DVD rip)

With several cues in the film a run draws only what a run from zero shows at its cut: nothing in the gap after a cue has ended, before the first cue or after the last, and the later cue (not the earlier) when it begins inside the second of two
A PGS picture built by more than one packet (a line added while an earlier line stays on screen) is drawn whole by a run that begins after the later packet, as a run from zero draws it

A run that begins where no cue is showing, 50 s or more after the last cue ended, reads no more bytes of the film before its first segment than the same run without the track (within the spread of repeated runs), for each of PGS (ended by a clear packet), VobSub (ended by its duration) and DVB (whose clear packet carries a duration); measured through a worker's job

A run that begins inside a cue reads, beyond the same run without the track, at most the film from that cue's first packet to the cut; checked for a cue 8 s old and one 50 s old through a worker's job with the cue times as production supplies them, and the bound does not grow with the gap before the cue
A run from segment 0, and a run whose image track is a file beside the film, read nothing they do not read today

No job (from zero, a seek, a failover or a helper) starts or waits on a read of the whole film, or any read that grows with the film's length, to learn cue times: the first mid-film run on a film reads the same before its first segment for the same cue in a film four times as long
Two runs of one film that begin at once on two workers (two helpers, or a helper and a seek) each stay within one run's bound, and neither waits for a read the other makes

If learning the cue times takes a read that fails for a reason that is not the film's (a store error, a timeout, the job ending), the run does not go on as if nothing were showing: no segment is stored without a cue a run from zero draws, the failure is not remembered as the film's, and the read ends with its job

A film that lists no times for the track without a whole-film read (MPEG-TS; a Matroska written without cue points for the track) still starts no whole-film read: a mid-film run reads at most a stated look-back more than the run without the track, shows a cue that began within that look-back from its first frame, and an older cue is the one remaining gap, pinned by a test on both sides of the look-back
A film already in the library when the release is deployed (scanned by the previous release, its file unchanged) meets these criteria by the next scan at the latest, with no step by the operator
After a film's file is replaced by one whose cues fall at other times, a mid-film run draws and reads by the new file's cues, never the old file's

docs/transcoding.md records a seek's bytes read and time to first segment, measured through a worker on a film of stated size and bitrate, for origin/main and for this build: with no cue showing, inside a cue 8 s old and one 50 s old, and for the first mid-film run on a film as well as a later one; no check passes or fails on a duration

userStories.title: Replace wall-clock ratio bars in tests with checks of the mechanism
userStories.description: Tests that pass or fail on a timing ratio are the largest class of merge-queue escapes (.results escape records for JS-067, JS-024 and JS-072): they pass on a 16-core developer machine and fail on shared CI runners. Convert the existing ratio bars (internal/transcode/helpers_integration_test.go and others found by grep) to checks of what the code does, such as how many helpers ran or which segments each made.
acceptanceCriteria: A timing bar is any assertion a slower runner can fail on a right build: a measured duration with an upper bound, two measured durations compared, or a measured speed with a lower bound or a not-slow flag. None is left in the Go tiers, test/e2e or test/roles.sh, and every assertion the grep finds that compares a measured time or speed is accounted for as replaced or as a hang bound, with the reason.

At least these are bars and are replaced. internal/transcode: helpers_integration_test.go (63 s for three workers; the 60/80/90% bars of TestMoreWorkersFinishTheFilmSooner; the 9 s slowest wait after a killed helper; the 9 s seek into a helper's chunk), helpers_preempt_integration_test.go (9 s slowest wait), hdrcopy_media_integration_test.go (10x real time), failover_integration_test.go (7 s from SIGKILL to the replacement's first segment), chapter_jobs_integration_test.go (2 s subtitle), metrics_integration_test.go (speed 0.6 to 1.5, twice). internal/api: transcoding_info_integration_test.go (EncodeSpeed 0.1 to 0.6 and 1.5 to 6, not flagged at 3x, not below 1 while paused). test/e2e/transcode.mjs: 78 s to reach 60 s of film, and the 5 s and 6 s stand-stills.

Each replacement passes on the unchanged application code and fails on a faulty copy of it with that mechanism removed: one faulty copy for each mechanism named below, each failed by the new check alone and not by a clock, none committed.
Each replacement gives the same verdict on a slow runner: it passes with the test, its workers and their ffmpeg held to two CPUs, and no case is dropped or failed for the number of cores.
No test is deleted, and each test that held a bar keeps every assertion it made that reads no clock.

Workers sharing a slow film, checked with two workers and with three: every worker made segments, no segment was made by two jobs, and jobs on different workers were running at the same moment. It fails when no helper starts, and when the workers make their chunks one after another.

The 4K HDR10 copy with TrueHD: the run decoded and encoded no video frame, and ffmpeg was given the arguments that keep the TrueHD's decoding off the video's path. It fails on a copy that decodes or re-encodes the picture, and on one that decodes the audio in the video's path.

A killed worker's job: the replacement was claimed by the other worker before the dead worker's own lease would have run out, and every request of the viewer was answered. It fails on a build that waits the lease out.

A helper that is killed, a helper stopped for another viewer, and a seek into a helper's chunk: the check is which job made each segment of that chunk (a replacement on another worker from the first segment missing; the viewer's own job after a preemption; the helper itself on a seek, with no job started) and that no request of the viewer failed. Each fails on a build where that job does not make them.

A subtitle asked for while chapter pictures fill their slots: it was read while that many chapter jobs were still running and none had finished since it was asked for. It fails on a build where chapter pictures may take every slot.

A shown speed (EncodeSpeed and Framerate in TranscodingInfo on both replicas, jellyscale_transcode_job_speed_ratio) is checked against what the worker recorded for the job, and against itself across a pause at the lead (not lower after than before); IsBelowRealTime is checked against that speed for one job the test keeps below 1 and one it keeps above. No check needs the runner to encode faster than the film.

In test/e2e/transcode.mjs the parallel and failover scenarios judge by what happened: a helper on another worker made segments past the seam that the player then played, the surviving worker took the job over, no request failed or was abandoned, no error dialog showed, and the buffer has no gap at the seam.

Every timing a bar measured is still measured and logged with what it is (the speedup of two and three workers over one, the copy's multiple of real time, kill to first segment, slowest wait, time to reach 60 s, longest stand-still); no test passes, fails or branches on one.

A time bound stays only where it stops a hang: a wait for an event with a timeout (waitFor, a context deadline, a select on time.After), or a measured bound of at least ten times what a right build takes at that step whose wrong build never delivers, or not before a timer or sleep the test set. A bound closer than that is a bar.
The change touches only test files, test scripts and docs: no file the server or a worker is built from.

docs/testing.md says that tests check mechanisms, not speeds, gives the rule for a time bound that may stay, and names where a run's logged timings are kept; what it says holds for a run that passed, locally and in CI.

userStories.title: CI's required checks cannot pass by being skipped, and protection has one source
userStories.description: roles has no aggregator, so a skipped roles satisfies the requirement; branch protection lives in both a ruleset and a classic rule that can drift; a pull request touching .github/ or test/**/*.sh is first exercised in the queue; any label restarts a pull request's run.

A pull request touching .github/ or test/**/*.sh runs the media tiers as ci:full does, and only the ci:full label restarts a run

userStories.title: Find and fix the recurring CI flakes
userStories.description: Recurring failures with no known cause: the POSIX burn-in of PGS (and VobSub) after far seeks in the subtitles e2e gate (the video element null, or playback stalled past 22 s; 3 queue runs, 2 PRs, and locally); and an ffprobe 'Stream ends prematurely' in a fault-injection test of PR 96. Hunt each under CI's cpuset with E2E_REPEAT or -count, decide whether it is a product race or a test bug, and fix the cause; never by a retry or a skip.
acceptanceCriteria: Each named failure is reproduced under CI's cpuset or shown not to reproduce in 20 runs, with its cause recorded
Each cause is fixed with a test that fails without the fix
The failure ledger (C/D) shows no repeat of either over the next ten merges

userStories.title: Search suggestions: GET /Search/Hints answers as Jellyfin 12.4 does
userStories.description: GET /Search/Hints answers 404, so a client that shows suggestions while the viewer types, Fluster among them (#102), shows none. compat/coverage-12.4.tsv calls it out of scope because jellyfin-web never calls it; Fluster, the client that ships with jellyscale, does. Observe Jellyfin 12.4's answer first.
acceptanceCriteria: GET /Search/Hints with searchTerm, limit, includeItemTypes=Movie,Series,Episode and userId (the signed-in viewer's), and no recursive, parentId or fields parameter, answers 200 in Jellyfin 12.4's SearchHintResult shape, observed on a real Jellyfin 12.4: one hint for each matching film, series and episode, with several matches of one type as well as one
A term typed part-way and in another case (a lowercase fragment of a title) finds the item, and an item whose name does not hold the term is never a hint
includeItemTypes narrows the hints to the types it names: Series alone answers the matching series and none of its episodes or any film
With more matches than limit the answer holds exactly limit hints, and TotalRecordCount is what Jellyfin 12.4 answers for the same request (observed: every match, or the page)
Each episode hint carries its own season as ParentIndexNumber and its own number as IndexNumber, checked on an episode where the two differ (S01E02 or S02E01), not only on S01E01

Each hint's PrimaryImageTag is the tag GET /Items/{itemId} gives that item in ImageTags.Primary, for a film, an episode and a series that has a picture; an item with no picture has no PrimaryImageTag (absent or null, never an empty string)
A term that matches nothing answers 200 with SearchHints an empty list (a list, not null) and TotalRecordCount 0
A request with no searchTerm, or an empty one, answers the status observed on Jellyfin 12.4 and never the whole library
A request without a token, and one with a token no device holds, is refused with the status observed on Jellyfin 12.4 (recorded in a capture) and gets no hints

An answer holding at least one film, one series and one episode hint passes the JS-070 schema checker (compat/conform) as SearchHintResult: SearchHints and TotalRecordCount present, and Artists, Id, ItemId, Name and Type in every hint

compat/coverage-12.4.tsv marks GET /Search/Hints done with evidence that names Fluster's call (#102) in place of 'nothing calls it', compat/endpoints.yaml lists the route as implemented, docs/status.md no longer lists it among the routes answered 404, and go test ./compat passes

The differential tier sends a GET /Search/Hints request whose term matches at least one film, one series and one episode of the fixtures to both servers, fails when either answers no hints, and compares which hints come back and their order; every difference left is listed in compat/differences.yaml under that request's name with its kind and reason
userStories.notes: Fluster, the client that ships with jellyscale (owner, 2026-11-12).

userStories.title: Recommendations from each viewer's own history, with a reason for each
userStories.description: Fluster, the client that ships with jellyscale, asked (#110) for 'Because you watched...' suggestions. The owner decided (2026-11-12) to build them as the first feature beyond Jellyfin's API: a per-account viewer profile built from watch history on the user's own server, computed by workers and stored in Postgres, with nothing sent outside it, served under the jellyscale namespace (/jellyscale/v1/, PRODUCT.md, #112) that unmodified clients never see. It needs watch history that survives scans (JS-076) and the library's genres, people and similar items (JS-046, JS-049).
acceptanceCriteria: A worker builds and updates each account's viewer profile from that account's watch history only, and nothing leaves the server

GET /jellyscale/v1/recommendations (authenticated as a Jellyfin token) answers suggestions for the signed-in viewer, each with a stated reason ('Because you watched X', a shared genre or person), documented and versioned
No Jellyfin route changes behaviour, and an unmodified Jellyfin client never sees the namespace
A viewer with no history gets a sensible answer (empty or popular in the library), and another account's history never shapes a viewer's suggestions
userStories.notes: First feature under /jellyscale/v1/; Fluster adopts it first.
